Methods for estimating average treatment effects

November 17, 2026

Source: vignettes/ATE-theory.Rmd
ATE-theory.Rmd

This vignette describes how atefit() estimates population-average treatment effects for binary, count and survival outcomes, including the outcome and treatment models, assumptions and bootstrap inference. Chapter 5 discusses marginal and conditional causal effects (Nguyen et al. 2026). For CATE score development and validation, see Methods for developing and validating CATE scores.

We use outcome model for the model of the outcome given treatment and covariates, treatment model for the model of treatment assignment given covariates, and censoring model for the model used to account for censoring in survival analyses. For binary treatment, the treatment model estimates the probability of treatment 1, also called the propensity score. These terms reflect the roles of the models discussed in causal inference, including Hernán and Robins (2020). The argument names ps.model and ipcw.model refer to the treatment and censoring models, respectively.

Average treatment effect for binary outcomes

For a fully observed binary outcome, atefit(response = "binary") estimates a population-average risk difference using augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW). This section describes the overall ATE; it does not describe binary CATE scoring or validation. See Kurz (2022) for an introduction to AIPW and its double-robustness property, and Hoogland et al. (2021) for treatment effect prediction with binary endpoints.

Estimand and assumptions

For patient ii, let Ri∈{0,1}R_i\in\{0,1\} denote treatment, Yi∈{0,1}Y_i\in\{0,1\} the observed outcome, and 𝐗i\boldsymbol X_i the baseline covariates. The outcome must be observed for all patients at the chosen, common follow-up horizon; the binary estimator does not adjust for censoring. Let Yi(r)Y_i^{(r)} denote the potential outcome under treatment rr. The marginal ATE on the risk difference scale is

Δ=𝔼[Y(1)]−𝔼[Y(0)]=μ1−μ0.\Delta = \mathbb E[Y^{(1)}] - \mathbb E[Y^{(0)}] = \mu_1 - \mu_0.

For an outcome coded as a favorable response, Δ>0\Delta>0 means a higher response probability under treatment 1; for an adverse outcome, it means a higher adverse-event probability. For example, 0.10 is a difference of 10 percentage points. A causal interpretation requires consistency, no unmeasured treatment–outcome confounding given the adjustment covariates, and positivity (both treatments must be possible at relevant covariate values). Chapter 5 introduces marginal and conditional effects (Nguyen et al. 2026).

Outcome and treatment models

Write mr(𝐱)=Pr⁡(Y=1∣R=r,𝐗=𝐱)m_r(\boldsymbol x)=\Pr(Y=1\mid R=r,\boldsymbol X=\boldsymbol x) and π(𝐱)=Pr⁡(R=1∣𝐗=𝐱)\pi(\boldsymbol x)=\Pr(R=1\mid\boldsymbol X=\boldsymbol x). outcome_model specifies the outcome and covariates for binomial logistic outcome models, fitted separately in each treatment arm. The resulting m̂0(𝐗i)\hat m_0(\boldsymbol X_i) and m̂1(𝐗i)\hat m_1(\boldsymbol X_i) predict response for every patient under each treatment.

ps.model specifies treatment and covariates for the treatment model. The default ps.method = "glm" uses logistic regression; "lasso" uses the package’s LASSO propensity procedure. Write the fitted treatment-1 propensity as π̂i\hat\pi_i. It is truncated to [minPS, maxPS], by default [0.01, 0.99], before calculating the treatment weights. For a randomized trial an intercept-only treatment model can be specified as trt ~ 1.

Augmented inverse probability weighting

For each arm, atefit() averages the predicted outcome plus an inverse-propensity-weighted residual correction:

μ̂1=1n∑i=1n[m̂1(𝐗i)+Riπ̂i{Yi−m̂1(𝐗i)}],\hat\mu_1 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left[ \hat m_1(\boldsymbol X_i) + \frac{R_i}{\hat\pi_i} \{Y_i-\hat m_1(\boldsymbol X_i)\}\right],

μ̂0=1n∑i=1n[m̂0(𝐗i)+1−Ri1−π̂i{Yi−m̂0(𝐗i)}],Δ̂=μ̂1−μ̂0.\hat\mu_0 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left[ \hat m_0(\boldsymbol X_i) + \frac{1-R_i}{1-\hat\pi_i} \{Y_i-\hat m_0(\boldsymbol X_i)\}\right],\qquad \hat\Delta=\hat\mu_1-\hat\mu_0.

The returned risk1, risk0, and risk.difference contain these estimates. The outcome and treatment models are fitted using the same analysis sample; this binary ATE implementation does not cross-fit them. Unlike a weighted identity-link regression coefficient, the estimated contrast above is obtained by subtracting two augmented population means. The construction is the same kind of augmented mean used for count outcomes, with response probabilities and their difference replacing rates and their ratio.

Under the identification assumptions and suitable regularity conditions, the estimator is consistent if either the treatment-specific outcome models are correctly specified or the treatment model is correctly specified (Kurz 2022). This does not protect against unmeasured confounding, poor overlap, or misspecification of both models. In particular, if truncation changes the true propensity scores, consistency based solely on a correctly specified treatment model is not guaranteed. The augmented estimates of μ0\mu_0 and μ1\mu_1 are not constrained to [0,1][0,1], nor is their difference constrained to [−1,1][-1,1].

Average treatment effect for count outcomes

For count outcomes, atefit(response = "count") estimates the population-level ratio of event rates for treatment 1 versus treatment 0. Let YiY_i be the event count observed during exposure Ti>0T_i>0, RiR_i the treatment, and 𝐗i\boldsymbol X_i the baseline covariates. The target is a ratio of population-average rates, rather than a conditional Poisson regression rate ratio. Identification requires appropriate treatment exchangeability, positivity, consistency and assumptions about the observation time and the relationship between counts and exposure.

Outcome and treatment models

outcome_model specifies the count outcome and covariates; an offset(log(T)) accounts for exposure. The outcome model is Poisson with a log link by default (outcome_method = "poisson"). Set outcome_method = "negative_binomial" (or "negbin") to use a negative binomial outcome model. Separate outcome models are fitted in each treatment arm; negative binomial dispersion is estimated separately in each arm. Predicted rates per unit of exposure are written m̂r(𝐗i)\hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i), for r=0,1r=0,1. A treatment model estimates π̂i=Pr⁡(Ri=1∣𝐗i)\hat\pi_i=\Pr(R_i=1\mid\boldsymbol X_i); as for binary outcomes, its fitted values are truncated using minPS and maxPS.

Augmented rate estimates

Using the notation for the binary ATE above, the augmented estimate of the rate for treatment rr is

λ̂r=1n∑i=1n[m̂r(𝐗i)+𝟏(Ri=r)p̂ri{YiTi−m̂r(𝐗i)}],\hat\lambda_r = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[ \hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i) + \frac{\mathbf{1}(R_i=r)}{\hat p_{ri}} \left\{\frac{Y_i}{T_i}-\hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i)\right\}\right],

where p̂1i=π̂i\hat p_{1i}=\hat\pi_i and p̂0i=1−π̂i\hat p_{0i}=1-\hat\pi_i. The output contains rate1, rate0, and the log rate ratio log⁡(λ̂1/λ̂0)\log(\hat\lambda_1/\hat\lambda_0) as log.rate.ratio. Exponentiating the latter gives the estimated rate ratio. This uses the same augmented-mean structure as the binary estimator, but the outcome is a rate and the contrast is a ratio.

Under the relevant identification and regularity assumptions, the augmented rates are consistent if either the outcome-rate model or the treatment model is correctly specified. This does not remove the need for appropriate exposure assumptions, overlap, or control of confounding. Truncating propensity scores can affect the guarantee based on the treatment model. A rate ratio is undefined when the estimated rates do not yield a valid positive ratio.

Average treatment effect for survival outcomes

For survival outcomes, atefit(response = "survival") estimates population summaries at a chosen horizon τ0\tau_0. For treatment rr, let T(r)T^{(r)} be the potential event time. Restricted mean survival time (RMST) is μr(τ0)=𝔼[min⁡{T(r),τ0}]\mu_r(\tau_0)=\mathbb E[\min\{T^{(r)},\tau_0\}], and restricted mean time lost (RMTL) is τ0−μr(τ0)\tau_0-\mu_r(\tau_0). The main treatment contrast is the log RMTL ratio

log⁡(τ0−μ1(τ0)τ0−μ0(τ0)).\log\!\left(\frac{\tau_0-\mu_1(\tau_0)}{\tau_0-\mu_0(\tau_0)}\right).

The function also reports the population-average event risk difference (treatment 1 minus treatment 0) and a population-level cumulative hazard ratio at the horizon, derived from the treatment-specific marginal survival probabilities. These summaries have different interpretations from a conditional Cox hazard ratio.

Outcome, treatment and censoring models

By default, the outcome model fits a Cox model separately in each treatment arm. Alternatively, outcome_method = "weibull" or "log_normal" fits an arm-specific accelerated failure time model. The Weibull model assumes proportional hazards across covariates within each arm, but different arm shapes allow non-proportional hazards between arms. The log-normal model does not impose proportional hazards. Both alternatives require their parametric event-time distributions to be appropriate. Each outcome model supplies predictions of each patient’s RMST and survival probability at τ0\tau_0 under each treatment. A treatment model estimates treatment probabilities, and a censoring model provides inverse probability of censoring weights (IPCW). The censoring model is controlled by ipcw.model, ipcw.method, and surv.min; the treatment model and truncation use the same controls described above. Because censoring can leave the event time unobserved, causal interpretation requires appropriate censoring assumptions and sufficient follow-up in addition to the treatment identification assumptions.

Augmented RMST and RMTL estimates

Let Ui=min⁡(Yi,τ0)U_i=\min(Y_i,\tau_0) be the observed time restricted at the horizon, m̂r(𝐗i)\hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i) the arm-specific predicted RMST, and p̂ri\hat p_{ri} the estimated probability of receiving treatment rr. Let wiw_i be the implemented IPCW weight for an observed restricted outcome, normalized to have mean one. The implementation computes

μ̂r=1n∑im̂r(𝐗i)+∑iwi𝟏(Ri=r){Ui−m̂r(𝐗i)}/p̂ri∑i𝟏(Ri=r)/p̂ri.\hat\mu_r = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i) + \frac{\sum_i w_i\mathbf{1}(R_i=r)\{U_i-\hat m_r(\boldsymbol X_i)\}/\hat p_{ri}} {\sum_i\mathbf{1}(R_i=r)/\hat p_{ri}}.

It reports rmst1, rmst0, and log.rmtl.ratio computed from these estimates. Under appropriate assumptions, including a correctly specified censoring model, the RMST estimator is doubly robust with respect to the outcome and treatment models. Propensity-score truncation can affect that property. If an augmented RMST lies outside [0,τ0][0,\tau_0], the implementation warns and substitutes the average outcome-model prediction for that arm; this fallback is not doubly robust.

Cumulative hazard ratio

The function also constructs augmented marginal survival estimates Ŝ0(τ0)\hat S_0(\tau_0) and Ŝ1(τ0)\hat S_1(\tau_0) using arm-specific outcome-model survival predictions, treatment weights and censoring weights. For valid survival estimates strictly between zero and one, it reports

log⁡(−log⁡Ŝ1(τ0)−log⁡Ŝ0(τ0))\log\!\left(\frac{-\log\hat S_1(\tau_0)}{-\log\hat S_0(\tau_0)}\right)

as log.cumulative.hazard.ratio. This population-level ratio of cumulative hazards at τ0\tau_0 is not a conditional Cox hazard ratio. If either estimated survival probability is outside (0,1)(0,1), the ratio is undefined rather than clipped to a valid range.

Bootstrap inference and assessment

For each outcome type, atefit() resamples patients with replacement n.boot times and refits the models used for estimation in each sample. It uses the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates as the standard error and reports a normal Wald confidence interval and a two-sided Wald p-value. The default 95% interval is θ̂±1.96SÊ\hat\theta \pm 1.96\,\widehat{SE}. confint() uses the stored standard error for other confidence levels without repeating the bootstrap. Supplying seed makes the resampling reproducible.

The effect scale depends on the outcome: bootstrap inference is on the risk difference for binary outcomes, the log rate ratio for counts, and, for survival, the log RMTL ratio, log cumulative hazard ratio, and event risk difference at the horizon. Exponentiate the log-ratio estimates and interval limits to obtain ratios. Treatment-specific bootstrap estimates are also retained and can be visualized with plot().

Failed or non-finite bootstrap estimates are recorded in bootstrap.diagnostics, including the replicate, affected measure and reason; diagnostics() also exposes these records. A warning summarizes the number of replicates and reasons. Inference for an affected measure is unavailable if any of its replicates is undefined; it is not calculated from only successful samples. Other measures with complete replicates can still have inference. For survival outcomes, the function also reports RMST outcome-model fallbacks in bootstrap samples, which are retained in the bootstrap inference.

Before interpreting an estimate, assess the treatment and outcome model covariates, treatment overlap, propensity-score truncation, fitting warnings and bootstrap stability. For survival outcomes, also assess censoring and support at the chosen horizon. These checks do not establish the absence of unmeasured confounding or prove that a model is correctly specified. Confidence intervals quantify sampling uncertainty under the estimation procedure, not uncertainty about unmeasured confounding or model misspecification. Bootstrap inference for an ATE is not validation of a CATE score.
